problems.description: Test fixture mutates module-level app_module.DATABASE global instead of using Flask app config; combined with the sys.path.insert hack this couples tests to implementation details and bypasses the app's own configuration seam.

test_list_tasks_ordered_desc relies on time.sleep(0.01) to disambiguate ordering, but created_at uses datetime.utcnow().isoformat() with second precision, so rows created in the same second tie — ordering assertion may be flaky outside the assumed ORDER BY.

Repo convention score is 0.68 with 14 violations (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE in app.py, celery_config.py, __init__.py, base.py); none of these files' violations are introduced by this diff (only app.py line 53 changes), so the commit inherits but does not worsen the score.

strengths: Fixes a real correctness bug: new tasks were persisted with status 'done', now correctly 'pending'
Adds 12 focused tests covering success, persistence, validation (missing/empty/no body), 404s, and partial updates
SonarQube delta is clean: +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0 cognitive complexity, +0.0% duplications
Diff is minimal and surgical — a one-line fix plus a self-contained test file with no collateral changes
commit_reviews.summary: A surgical bug fix ('done'->'pending') backed by thorough pytest coverage that clearly improves the codebase, though it inherits the repo's pre-existing low convention score (0.68) and adds minor test-hygiene debt (global DATABASE mutation, sleep-based ordering) — but these are not introduced by this diff.

problems.description: fetch_task is documented as the alias for legacy clients, yet its signature was changed to require owner_id, breaking the very callers the alias exists for; the same ripple applies to create_task/get_tasks/get_task/update_task.
No test changes for a +364-line auth feature (AST diff shows +1 file, +0 test files): register/login/token validation, owner_id scoping, and the schema migration are all untested.
JWT signing falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' SECRET_KEY; acceptable for a dev baseline but a real token-forgery risk if deployed as-is.
Adds 4 imports including a new `jwt` dependency and werkzeug.security; the diff does not show a requirements change, so the build may break in clean environments.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+ and removed in 3.13; used in generate_token and create_task.
token_required mutates the request object via request.user_id to pass state to handlers, an implicit coupling that the flat-function style doesn't otherwise use.

Mechanical convention score (0.68, 14 violations) is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, __init__.py, base.py); the commit's own code uses snake_case functions and UPPER_CASE constants correctly.

strengths: Data-preserving _migrate_add_owner_id migration (PRAGMA column check + ALTER TABLE) instead of dropping existing task data.
Coherent auth addition that respects the existing single-file Flask structure, section-comment headers, and get_db() pattern.
All task queries are scoped by owner_id (SELECT/UPDATE ... AND owner_id = ?), which is correct multi-tenant isolation.
Correct decorator ordering (@app.route outer, @token_required inner) and proper HTTP status codes (400/401/409/201) with distinct expired/invalid token errors.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured auth feature that fits the existing flat Flask architecture and preserves data via a safe migration, but introduces debt through untested code, a breaking change to the legacy fetch_task alias, and a hardcoded JWT secret.

problems.description: The notification is enqueued synchronously in the request path via .delay() with no fallback; if the Celery broker is unreachable the endpoint can 500 even though the task update already persisted. Status change and notification are not atomic.
send_notification_email is called with owner['username'] bound to the user_email parameter; the identifier is a username, not an email address, so the 'email' would be addressed to the wrong field.
Completion-transition side effect is embedded directly in the edit_task route handler rather than a service layer or post-update hook, coupling notification logic to the HTTP layer.
Test setup (calls list + monkeypatch + create helper) is duplicated across all five new tests; a shared fixture would reduce repetition.
Module-level constants in celery_config.py (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes) are lowercase; should be UPPER_CASE per the analyzer's own rule.

Flagged discrepancy: several reported convention violations (base.py, __init__.py) reference files not touched in this diff, and function/class violations are attributed to celery_config.py which contains no functions or classes — likely pre-existing or analyzer misattribution, not introduced here.

strengths: Transition detection (previous vs new status) correctly prevents duplicate notifications and no-ops on non-completed statuses or title-only edits.
Notification is fetched within the owner's user scope, preserving the existing authorization boundary.
Async email decoupled into a Celery task keeps I/O out of the request path, and no new bugs/smells/duplications were introduced (only +4 cognitive complexity).
Thorough edge-case test coverage with monkeypatched .delay(), including the no-retrigger and response-unaffected cases.
Test file grouping and route+direct-DB-function style match the existing codebase patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, edge-case-aware integration that cleanly adds async owner notification on task completion, marred only by minor issues (synchronous enqueue with no broker fallback, username-vs-email mismatch, and lowercase Celery constants).

problems.description: fetch_task() is retained as a legacy alias to task_repository.get() with a docstring claiming 'legacy clients' use it, but the app is self-contained; if nothing calls it this is dead compatibility code that should be removed once callers are updated.

Repositories are instantiated at module import time (user_repository = UserRepository(get_db)) rather than per-request or via lazy construction, coupling repository lifecycle to app import time; acceptable for a small Flask app but limits testability/DI.

Static analysis flags 14 convention violations (score 0.68) including snake_case functions and non-PascalCase classes in newly-added modules (celery_config.py, base.py, __init__.py), even though the core repositories.py code itself follows naming conventions.

strengths: Clean repository extraction (TaskRepository/UserRepository) that centralizes all SQL and moves schema creation and migration out of the app module.
Public API surface preserved — route paths, status codes, and response shapes unchanged, and the legacy fetch_task alias keeps backward compatibility.
Migration logic is preserved as create_schema/migrate_schema rather than dropped, so existing databases are not broken.
Dependency injection via the get_db callable factory decouples repositories from global connection state.
commit_reviews.summary: This is a net-positive architectural refactor that introduces a repository layer and preserves the existing API surface and data, but carries minor convention violations in new support modules and a legacy alias that may be dead code.

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.68 is dragged down almost entirely by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, __init__.py, base.py); this commit's own additions are snake_case-clean and +0 classes, so the score understates the change's actual convention hygiene.

_storage_options() embeds a test-only fakeredis seam in production app.py behind a FAKE_REDIS env var; injecting storage via test config or monkeypatching would keep production code free of test concerns (though it is isolated and documented).
Every paginated request runs an extra COUNT(*) total query, adding a full scan per page; total is rarely required by clients and is optional for cursor pagination.

list_for_owner contract changed from a bare list to a pagination envelope, and sort switched from created_at to id (equivalent only while ids are monotonic); reasonable for an evolving story API but breaks existing consumers.

strengths: Correct keyset/cursor pagination with limit+1 lookahead and stable id ordering, avoiding OFFSET scalability issues
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user_id with IP fallback and a single shared application_limits budget across endpoints
Clean JSON 429 handler plus integer validation with 400s and MAX_PAGE_LIMIT clamping
Hermetic tests via fakeredis with limiter.reset() isolation; existing tests updated and new pagination tests added
Well-documented design rationale in comments (application_limits vs default_limits, storage seam)
Introduces no new bugs and only 1 smell despite +29 cognitive complexity, which is proportionate to the two features
commit_reviews.summary: Well-architected cross-cutting commit adding correct cursor pagination and user-aware rate limiting with solid tests; the low convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this change's own code.

compounding_issues: Hardcoded JWT_SECRET fallback ('development-secret-change-me') introduced in Session 2 and never hardened in later sessions
Schema evolution via ALTER TABLE + PRAGMA column checks (owner_id in S2, email in S3) carried as an idempotency hack instead of a proper migration layer
f-string SQL column/table interpolation in repositories (inherited from the S1 model code) persisted unchanged through the Session 4 refactor
Hardcoded redis://localhost:6379/0 defaults for Celery broker, result backend, and rate-limiter storage — conflicts with the framework rule that 6379 is never to be used
Rate limiter is bound to the Flask app at import time as a module-level singleton, forcing the test fixture to call limiter.reset() and keeping the seam indirect
key_decisions: Session 1: rewrote the seed into a clean single-file Flask app with strict JSON-body validation and init_db() at module scope so WSGI/test imports work
Session 2: JWT auth via a token_required decorator plus owner_id scoping on every task query, with a legacy-user migration so pre-existing tasks stay accessible after the ownership change
Session 3: Celery async email notifications exposed through a send_notification_email.delay() seam in a separate celery_config.py, keeping side effects async and mockable
Session 4: behavior-preserving extraction of a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), cutting app.py by ~200 lines with the public API unchanged
Session 5: cursor-based pagination with strict limit/cursor validation and per-user rate limiting keyed on the authenticated JWT subject with IP fallback
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across all five sessions. Session 1 delivered a minimal, well-validated CRUD API with a small test suite; Session 2 layered JWT auth and per-user data isolation on top without regressions; Session 3 added async Celery notifications with thorough mocking coverage; Session 4 consolidated the growing monolith into a repository package while keeping every existing test green; and Session 5 closed with well-tested cross-cutting concerns (pagination, rate limiting, error handling) that extend the repository seam cleanly. Test coverage grew in lockstep at every commit and all 9 tests pass in the final state, so the closing sessions reinforced rather than eroded the structure built in sessions 1-2.
story_review.summary: A textbook greenfield-to-auth-to-integration-to-refactor-to-cross-cutting progression where each session built naturally on its predecessor, expanded the test suite in lockstep, and the final sessions paid down structure without breaking a single test.
